reason: The sources provide 15 distinct, doubly-sourced claims regarding the discovery, dimensions, and potential origins of the Fermi bubbles.
story: In 2010, astronomers analyzing public data from NASA’s Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope discovered something massive hiding in plain sight. Masked by a fog of background radiation were two gargantuan, symmetric lobes of energetic plasma now known as Fermi bubbles. These structures tower 25,000 light-years above and below the Milky Way’s center, spanning a total of 50,000 light-years—roughly half the diameter of our entire galaxy. Emitting high-energy gamma and X-rays, these bubbles were likely born from a violent outburst at the galaxy's heart. One theory suggests the supermassive black hole, Sagittarius A*, blasted out powerful jets after a massive feeding event. Another possibility is a period of intense star formation and supernovae that occurred millions of years ago. Though invisible to the naked eye, these colossal bubbles prove the Milky Way isn't as quiet as it looks; it is a galaxy that breathes fire into the deep void.
angle: The Milky Way is hiding two gargantuan bubbles of radiation that tower 25,000 light-years high, invisible to the eye but spanning half the diameter of the galaxy.

claims.claim: The Fermi bubbles were discovered in November 2010.
The structures consist of two large elliptical lobes of energetic plasma.
The bubbles extend approximately 25,000 light-years above and below the Galactic Center.
The total span of the bubbles is approximately 50,000 light-years.
The bubbles emit high-energy gamma rays.
The discovery was led by Douglas Finkbeiner, along with Meng Su and Tracy Slatyer.
The bubbles were identified using data from NASA's Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope.
The telescope's Large Area Telescope (LAT) was used to chart the gamma-ray sources.
The bubbles were previously hidden by a 'fog' of diffuse gamma-ray emission in the Milky Way's disk.
One potential origin for the bubbles is the supermassive black hole Sagittarius A*.
The black hole may have produced high-energy jets to form the bubbles.
An alternative theory suggests the bubbles were caused by a burst of star formation.
The bubbles span a distance roughly half the diameter of the Milky Way galaxy.
The lobes of the Fermi bubbles are symmetric in shape.

disputed: The primary cause of the bubbles is disputed between activity from the Sagittarius A* black hole and a recent burst of star formation (S1, S6).
The acceptance of Finkbeiner's previous microwave 'haze' detection in WMAP data was not fully accepted by other team members, unlike the Fermi discovery (S6).
